draft.title: Other pressures on parliament
card: Parliament does not make laws in isolation. Outside forces shape what laws it can make and what laws it is willing to make.
International pressure

Australia signs treaties, which are agreements with other countries. A treaty does not become Australian law until parliament passes a statute to put it into effect. Once it does, the Commonwealth may use its external affairs power to make laws on the treaty's subject.
Other countries and bodies
Governments and international bodies can also press Australia to change a law, for example through public criticism or trade and diplomatic pressure.
Voters

MPs want to be re-elected. They tend to avoid laws voters strongly oppose and are more willing to pass laws voters want. Voters can influence parliament through elections, petitions, media and lobbying.
draft.remember: Treaties and voters both shape parliament: treaties help set what it can do, and voters influence what it will do.

a.q: Australia signs a treaty on protecting wetlands. What must happen before it becomes part of Australian law?
opts: Parliament passes a statute to give it effect
The Prime Minister signs it on behalf of Australia
The other countries to the treaty vote to approve it
The High Court declares that it applies in Australia
a.why: A treaty binds Australia internationally, but it becomes Australian law only when parliament passes a statute to put it into effect. Signing alone is tempting but is not enough, because signing is done by the executive and is not law-making.
a.clue: Who makes statute law in Australia?

b.q: A government has a bill that polls show most voters strongly oppose. Which is the most likely effect of voter opinion on parliament?
opts: The government may change or drop the bill to keep votes
The bill is invalid because voters have not approved it
The Governor-General must refuse royal assent to the bill
The High Court must strike the bill out before it is passed
b.why: Governments want to be re-elected, so strong voter opposition can lead them to change or drop a bill. Voter opinion does not make a bill invalid or force any court or official to block it. It is a political pressure and not a legal rule.
b.clue: Think about what MPs need at the next election.

a.best: Parliament passes a statute to give it effect

b.best: The government may change or drop the bill to keep votes

problems.detail: The card gets the external affairs power backwards. It says that once parliament passes a statute, the Commonwealth 'may use its external affairs power'. In fact the external affairs power (s 51(xxix)) is what lets the Commonwealth pass the statute that implements the treaty in the first place. The statute does not unlock the power.

The remember line sorts the ideas more neatly than the card does: treaties set what parliament 'can' do and voters what it 'will' do. The card only says outside forces shape both. International pressure, which the card covers, also affects what parliament is willing to do.
The clue 'Who makes statute law in Australia?' uses 'statute', which appears only in the right option. A student can match the word without knowing the idea.
The right option is the only one with a soft qualifier ('may'). The three distractors all state absolutes ('must', 'is invalid'), so the right answer stands out.

check.summary: The card wrongly says the external affairs power becomes available only after a statute is passed, when that power is what lets parliament pass the statute. Also: the remember line splits 'can' and 'will' more neatly than the card, question a's clue gives the answer away, and question b's right option stands out by being the only one with 'may'.
